description: Copies of a known template are hidden in white Gaussian noise at unknown delays. Cross-correlating the received signal with the template produces a peak at each delay. The MicroSim shows the template, its time-reversed matched filter, the correlation output with threshold detection and per-peak SNR, and a moving-average filter for comparison.

educational.topic: Cross-correlation and matched filtering for detection in noise
learningObjectives: Explain how cross-correlation locates a known pattern inside a longer signal
Relate the matched filter to the time-reversed template and to cross-correlation
Analyze how input SNR, template length and threshold affect missed detections and false alarms
Compare templates by the sharpness of their correlation peaks and the resulting timing accuracy

equations: peak SNR = E_s / sigma^2 = L x input SNR
assumptions: Noise is white and Gaussian, generated by a seeded pseudo-random generator
Input SNR is the average template power divided by the noise variance
Templates are real-valued, so no complex conjugate is needed in the matched filter
A detection within a quarter of the template length of a true delay counts as a hit

keyQuestions: Why can the correlator find a signal that is invisible in the received waveform?
How does the detection threshold trade missed signals against false alarms?
Why does a chirp give a more accurate delay estimate than a rectangular pulse of the same length?
commonMisconceptions: Any smoothing filter improves detection as well as a matched filter
A signal below the noise level cannot be detected
The matched filter output looks like the template
assessmentOpportunities: Compute the expected peak SNR from the input SNR and the template length
Tally missed signals and false alarms over ten noise records at two thresholds
